title: What If The Immortal Snail Chased You and Never Stopped?
description:
Hour Seven ⏳
What would you do if the unthinkable happened? Animated “what if” stories that put you in the moment, one second at a time.

🔔 Subscribe for new scenarios every week
📱 TikTok: @whatif_animations4u
📸 Instagram: @whatif_stories4u

Drop your own “what if” in the comments. Your idea might be next.



What If the Immortal Snail Was After You?
Someone offers you $10 million and eternal life. The only catch: an immortal snail crawls toward you at 0.03 mph, forever. If it touches you, you die. You say yes.
At first it's easy. You buy a car, you move cities, you fly to Hawaii. But the snail never sleeps, never stops, and never loses your trail. Years become decades, decades become centuries, and the world changes around you. Friends grow old, cities rise and fall, and you leave Earth itself. Billions of years later the sun dies, the last star burns out, and the universe goes cold and dark.
But the snail is immortal too.
The math we used: 0.03 mph = about 0.7 miles a day and 260 miles a year. Seattle to Hawaii (2,700 miles) ≈ 10 years. The opposite side of Earth (12,450 miles) ≈ 47 years. 4 light-years at snail speed ≈ 90 billion years.
Would you still take the deal? Comment YES or NO.

title: What If You Were Born as CJ? | GTA San Andreas
description:
You're a baby on Grove Street. No gang. No green. Not even a bike. Years later, your mom is killed in a drive-by, and you fly home from Liberty City. Before you even reach Grove Street, crooked cops take your money and dump you in enemy territory with nothing but a kid's bike. Then you take back your hood, steal a jetpack from a secret army base, and rob a Mafia casino. And the first friend to hug you when you came home? He's the one who sold you out. This is the whole life of Carl Johnson, from a kid who ran away to the man who finally came back, told as if it were yours.

Sweet, Big Smoke, Ryder, Officer Tenpenny, the green Sabre, the damn train, the jetpack, the casino, and a fire truck in the middle of Grove Street.

Would you have gone back to Grove Street? And which game character should be born next? Tell me in the comments.

description:

You wake up tomorrow, open your closet... and there's nothing in it. Not even socks. In this world, humans never invented clothes.

So we walked through seven rooms of that world: the cold, the sun, the office, the awkward part, the missing industry, space... and the morning Kevin had an idea.

Would you survive one day in this world? Tell us in the comments.

Real facts in this video
• Clothing is roughly 170,000 years old: body lice, which live in clothes, split from head lice around then. Toups et al., Molecular Biology and Evolution 28(1), 2011. https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msq234
• Below about 27 °C a resting naked body has to spend extra energy to stay warm (estimates of this lower critical temperature run 27–30 °C): Speakman & Keijer, Molecular Metabolism 2(1), 2013. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molmet.2012.10.002
• Earth's average temperature is about 15 °C: NASA Earth Fact Sheet. https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html
• Unprotected skin can be damaged by the sun in as little as 15 minutes: CDC, Sun Safety. https://www.cdc.gov/skin-cancer/sun-safety/
• More than 100 billion garments were made in 2014, nearly 14 for every person on Earth: McKinsey & Company, Style that's sustainable (2016). https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/sustainability/our-insights/style-thats-sustainable-a-new-fast-fashion-formula
• Richard Arkwright patented his water-powered spinning frame in 1769: Encyclopaedia Britannica. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Richard-Arkwright

Kevin, the squirrel and everyone else are fictional. Any resemblance to real Kevins is a coincidence.

title: What If You Could See Everyone's Future Height?
description:
What if you could see how tall everyone will be in the future? 📏👀

Imagine being 21 years old and only 5'8", while your 6'0" best friend constantly makes fun of your height.

title: What If You Had 500 Charisma?
description:
Would you take it? Play this episode's round of the What If Card Game free → https://whatifgame.site/d11

What if you had 500 charisma? You throw a dodgeball straight through the gym window, and Principal Hale, who has never smiled in her life, is already filling out your detention slip. You ask about her fish. Twenty minutes later, the window was nobody's fault, and you walk out with the keys to the vending machine. Most people have about ten charisma. You have five hundred.

At first it's amazing. Mom says yes to a dog after six years of no. The pop quiz turns open-book. The kid who's taken your hat since fourth grade starts carrying your backpack to the bus. The mayor builds a skatepark with your name on it, the governor lets you steer his helicopter, and an envelope comes on White House paper: the President wants to meet you. Then you find out nobody can say no to you. Not even when they want to.

Everyone who has ever met you loves you. You just can't name one person who'd still like you if they had a choice.

Would you take it? Play this episode's round of the What If Card Game free → https://whatifgame.site/d11

What's the first thing you'd ask for? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- People make up their minds about a new face in about a tenth of a second. Judgments of trustworthiness, likeability and competence made after a 100-millisecond look were close to the ones made with no time limit; more time mostly made people more confident. Willis & Todorov (2006), "First impressions: Making up your mind after a 100-ms exposure to a face", Psychological Science 17(7).
- Students guessed they'd have to ask about 11 strangers before 3 agreed to write the word "pickle" in pen in a library book. On average they needed about 5, and 87% of them underestimated how many people would say yes. Bohns, Roghanizad & Xu (2014), "Underestimating our influence over others' unethical behavior and decisions", Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 40(3).
- After talking for the first time, people think the other person liked them less than they really did. Five studies, from strangers in a lab to college dorm mates. Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018), "The liking gap in conversations: Do people like us more than we think?", Psychological Science 29(11).
- The White House Easter Egg Roll draws tens of thousands of people: more than 30,000 in 2011, and about 40,000 in 2024, according to the White House. AP (2011, 2024).

title: What If Everyone Could Hear Your Thoughts?
description:
What If Everyone Could Hear Your Thoughts?
Would you take it? Now add the catch: …but it's ten times stronger at family dinners. Yes or hell no?We turned this question into a card game: the What If Card Game. 150 cards, and your friends pick your catch. Play this round free → https://whatifgame.site/p12

What if everyone near you could hear every thought in your head? You're halfway through a quiz when the girl in front of you turns around and asks for a pencil. You hand her one and keep your mouth shut. "She's so pretty." Every head in the room turns to you.

At first it's amazing. Your participation grade goes from a C to an A, and you never raise your hand. You win an argument with your little sister without saying a word. One bite of a taco and everybody in line orders three. Companies fly you in to test their toys, and the biggest pop star on the planet wants you on stage in front of twenty thousand people, because you're the one person who can't fake liking her song. Then your best friend hears what you really think.

You don't get to pick what you think. Nobody does. Everybody else just gets to keep it to themselves.

Would you take it? Now add the catch: …but it's ten times stronger at family dinners. Yes or hell no?
We turned this question into a card game: the What If Card Game. 150 cards, and your friends pick your catch.

Play this round free → https://whatifgame.site/p12

Who's the one person you'd never want hearing your thoughts? Tell us in the comments.

Is any of this real? The science in this episode:
- In 2025, Stanford scientists decoded sentences that four people with paralysis only imagined saying, using implants in the motor cortex. When participants silently counted shapes, the decoder picked up the numbers without being asked, so the team added an imagined password that keeps it off until it's thought. Kunz, Meschede-Krasa et al. (2025), Cell.
- People who wrote down every lie they told for a week told one or two a day on average, and about one in four was told only for the other person's sake. DePaulo, Kirkendol, Kashy, Wyer & Epstein (1996), "Lying in everyday life", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 70(5).
- People who said their thoughts out loud for five minutes while trying not to think of a white bear still thought of it more than once a minute. Wegner, Schneider, Carter & White (1987), "Paradoxical effects of thought suppression", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(1).
- Across 10 studies and more than 13,000 secrets, people's minds wandered to their secrets far more often than they ever had to hide them. Slepian, Chun & Mason (2017), "The experience of secrecy", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 113(1).
- The capital of Australia is Canberra, not Sydney. Australian Government, "Our country" (australia.gov.au).

description:

Stickman survival: a zombie survival story, day by day. A zombie outbreak hits a cruise ship four nights out, and you have to survive 100 days at sea. The full movie: all of Season 1 in one video.

Seven short blasts and one long. Everyone runs for the muster stations. You lock your cabin door instead, and you learn the one rule that keeps you alive: they follow the light. So you stay dark.

Day 0 to Day 100: a zombie ship drifting onto a reef. A lifeboat with the last of the water. A ghost ship in the fog, a radio, and a German shepherd named Biscuit. A zombie island, a lighthouse that calls the dead out of the sea, and a floating town of sixty boats where every light is burning.

Real survival facts all the way through: ship alarms, lifeboat rations, anchors, rip currents, finding water on an island, scurvy and tides.

title: What If You Had Infinite IQ in PRISON?
description:
You got ten years in prison for a robbery you didn't do. Six hours in, you've already found three ways out. You close the door anyway. Because the door you want is the front one, with a judge saying sorry.

What if you had infinite IQ in prison? Beat the dominoes king by listening to his knocks, invent paper money out of ramen, find 41 ways out of Blackrock and hand the warden the shopping list to fix them. Then read a store camera like a clock: one stop sign, one shadow, one bus window, and a clock nobody moved back an hour.

The gate was open. Ten steps. Nobody watching. Would you have walked back to the count line? Tell us in the comments.

This is a fictional What If story. Blackrock State Prison, its people and the case are made up. The facts in it are real:
- Ramen became the currency of a U.S. state prison, replacing stamps and cigarettes: Michael Gibson-Light, University of Arizona, American Sociological Association, 2016.
- A full double-six domino set has 28 tiles.
- A TV antenna is metal cut to a fraction of the wavelength it receives (a half-wave dipole); chip bags are lined with metal foil.
- China's first government paper money (jiaozi) appeared around 1023 AD, more than a thousand years after its first coins.
- In January 1906 Houdini escaped from Charles Guiteau's old cell in the U.S. Jail in Washington, D.C., then moved prisoners into other cells as a prank.
- Drones have been used to drop phones over prison walls in the U.S. since at least 2015; the DOJ Inspector General calls it a growing threat.
- Investigators date photos and videos by shadow length (chronolocation, Bellingcat). A 10-foot sign in early November casts roughly 27 feet of shadow at 3 p.m. and about twice that an hour later.
- U.S. daylight saving time ends on the first Sunday of November; security cameras that aren't reset run an hour off.
- City buses log their GPS position to the second (automatic vehicle location).
- About 2,900 home dryer fires happen each year in the U.S.; the leading cause is failure to clean the lint (U.S. Fire Administration).
- In a fire, smoke rises: the cleaner air is down low (NFPA, American Red Cross).
- More than 3,600 people have been exonerated in the U.S. since 1989 (National Registry of Exonerations, 3,646 by the end of 2024).

title: What IF You Saved Your School From a Shooting?
description:
What if you saved your school from a shooting? One ordinary morning becomes an emergency, and suddenly you’re worried about your friends, your teachers, and what might happen next. Could a quick decision help someone reach safety?

In this animated what-if story, we imagine a student facing a frightening situation: recognising danger, taking instructions seriously, and helping others without seeking out the threat. With confusion spreading and information incomplete, even understanding what’s happening could feel overwhelming.

What would it mean to help? It might be alerting a trusted adult, sharing important information with emergency responders, or supporting someone who’s frightened. Making a difference wouldn’t have to mean confronting an attacker—and nobody should have to face an emergency alone.

This serious animated story explores courage, teamwork, and the people who help a school community through its hardest moments. Beyond the headlines, we also consider what comes afterward: reconnecting with loved ones, supporting survivors, and finding help to recover.

What makes someone a hero in your eyes? Share your thoughts respectfully in the comments, and subscribe for more animated stories exploring difficult choices, human connections, and extraordinary situations.
